sections.heading: Lingaraja Temple
sections.content: The largest and most outstanding example of Nagara style of temple building at Bhubaneswar, the capital of Orissa and a city of temples is the Lingaraja Temple. Also Bhubaneswar has been referred to in several of ancient texts as a sacred pilgrimage center. Dedicated to Lord Shiva, Lingraja temple is almost a thousand year old. The Lingam here is a unique Hari Hara lingam  representation of half Shiva and half Vishnu. Located in a spacious courtyard and fortified walls, the temple has an elaborately carved vimana or tower which rises up to 180 feet and has several vertical sections, the recesses of which are filled with more miniature vimanas.The temple consists of a Nata Mandir, Bhog Mandapa and a Jagamohan. The spacious courtyard is full of shrines, big and small, built in different periods and their number exceeding a hundred, of which only a few are of outstanding merit. The complex is enclosed by a massive compound-wall having an imposing gateway on the east and two secondary gates on the north and south. There are more than 150 other shrines around the main temple. The Shivalinga in the sanctum is 8 inches above the floor level, and is 8 feet in diameter. The Bhagawati temple is located in the northwest corner of the courtyard. There are several other shrines and temples in this vast courtyard. The largest structure known as the Sri Mandir is studded with 65 temples of different sizes. Once a year, an image of Lingaraja is taken to the Jalamandir in the center of the Bindu Sagar lake in Bhubaneswar.

sections.heading: Rajarani Temple
sections.content: The Rajarani Temple was built between the tenth and eleventh century from reddish gold sandstone known as Rajarani in the local language. It is a graceful and elegant structure which boasts of intricately carved figurines performing everyday activities. The temple stands on a raised platform and its spire is decorated with clusters of turrets (replication of the spire itself) emerging form the rib of the spire. The jagmohana is extremely plain, and was repaired in 1903 after having fallen down in ruins. The deul, on the other hand, is spectacularly ornate, and is famous for the aesthetic concept of miniature temple spires clustered around the main tower. The sculptural images of the temple are elegant and lively, especially the beautiful female figures which are in amorous, as well as engaged in such activities as holding children, looking in mirrors, and playing with pet birds. On the lower register of the deul, on the corner projection, are found the famous 'Guardians of the Eight Directions'. From the gateway in a clockwise direction around the porch and the deul to end back at the torana the eight guardians are Indra (god of rain), Agni (god of fire), Yama (god of death), Nirriti (god of suffering), Varuna (god of ocean), Vayu (god of wind), Kubera (god of wealth) and Ishana (Shiva).This Temple is the only one of its kind in the region of Orissa to have a cluster of small sized towers, or shikharas, in tiers which together make the main tower. Both the jagamohana and the deul are richly decorated.

sections.heading: Mukteswara Temple
sections.content: Mukteswara temple is dedicated to Lord Shiva - Mukteswara and is carved with figures of ascetics in various postures of meditation. The relationship with older structures can be seen in the small size of the temple - 35 feet high. The latticed windows of the Jagmohana and the octagonal compound wall seems to have been patterned on an earlier structure, a torana (arched gateway), which was found in a field near Bhubaneswar during excavations. It is now in the Orissa State Museum. The extraordinarily beautiful sculptures include elaborate scrolls, graceful female figures, monkeys, peacocks, and a wealth of delicate carvings. Humorous and lively scenes depicting popular stories from the Panchatantra are carved around the windows of the Jagmohana. The image of a mythical lion head (shardul) with open jaws, flanked by attendants, over an elaborate horseshoe shaped chaitya is found on the southern exterior projecting wall of the tower and is a common feature of many later temples of Orissa. This is one of the first and the finest appearance of this image. There are a number of depictions of skeletal ascetics among the sculptural images, most of them shown in teaching or meditation. On the outer face of the compound wall are niches containing a variety of divinities. These include Saraswati (sitting on a lotus with two female attendants), Ganesa (with his attendant mouse), and Lakulisha (the fifth century founder of the Pashupata sect of tantric Shaivism), who is portrayed sitting cross-legged, with two miniature ascetic figures in the triangular side panels. Several small shrines with Lingam can be noticed within the compound.

sections.heading: Interesting Facts
sections.content: Dhauli hills are presumed to be the area of the bloody battle of Kalinga, won by the Mauryan emperor Ashoka in third cen. BCE. Though he conquered, his horrors of having slain over 1,50,000 people and the misery it inflicted on the people filled Ashoka with remorse and brought about a sudden change of heart. The great Mauryan king renouncing the path of violence embraced Buddhism and spread the dharma through rock edicts, installed in different parts around the empire.

sections.heading: Orissa- Monument- Dhauli
sections.content: Dhauli has major edicts of Ashoka engraved on a mass of rock. The edicts are remarkable and they have been excellently preserved, despite the fact that they date back to the 3rd century BC. The top of the rock is sculpted into an imposing elephant's head, which is the Buddha's mothers dream of the Buddha descending to her womb in the form of an elephant. The forepart of the elephant, hewn here out of solid rock represents the earliest sculpture tradition in Orissa. At Dhauli, Ashoka built several chaityas, stupas and pillars. This is said to be one of the earliest rock cut structure in India.

sections.heading: Orissa- Monument- Vikramkhol
sections.content: The rock art of Orissa dates back to as early as the prehistoric period, the earliest being the rock shelters of Vikramkhol dating to 1500 BC containing pre-historic, undeciphered pictographic inscriptions. The caves must have attracted people to live there, who decorated these rock shelters with paintings and engravings in various geometrical forms and figures of human and animal figurines. Drawn in monochromatic and polychromatic floral patterns they have withstood the test of time. The engravings still have traces of red ochre fillings.

sections.heading: Orissa- Monument- Cave Temples- Khandagiri and Udaygiri
sections.content: Khandagiri hills are known for fifteen rock cut caves while the Udaygiri hiils have eighteen caves. First among these is the Rani Gumpha. Used as a monastery it has corridors with a double row of pillars and a row of rectangular rooms. Above each entrance is an arch, resembling the torana reliefs. There are ruins of wooden temples on the hill. The Jain temple in Khandagiri belongs to the nineteenth century. In the caves around the temples, statues of various Tirthankaras sculpted between eleventh and fifteenth Century has been found.

sections.heading: Orissa- Monument- Ratnagiri
sections.content: Ratnagiri had been known as a centre for Buddhism during seventh to ninth century. It was also known for a university similar to Nalanda. On the peak of the hill, is the foundation of a stupa surrounded by a number of smaller stupas. There are also a small and a large monastery. The large monastery shows a dependence of the Gupta style of architecture, especially the Buddha carved around the entrance and on the doorway of the shrine. A number of Buddhist buildings were also excavated at Udaygiri. Statues from the Baumakara dynasty, a restored stupa with a chaumukha and a number of statues were also found there. A Buddhist monastery on the hill has a larger than life statue of Buddha enshrined in the central courtyard. There are beautiful sculptures on the pillars of the shrines entrance.

sections.heading: Konark Sun Temple
sections.content: Konark is the abode of a magnificent temple dedicated to the Sun God. Built by King Narasimhadeva in the thirteenth century to mark his victory over the Mughal invaders, it is a colossal structure. Though in a ruined state, it is an outstanding example reflecting the genius of the architects who envisioned and built it. Referred to as the Black Pagoda the ruins of this temple were excavated in late nineteenth century with the tower over the Garbhagriha missing, although the jagmohana is intact. Devoted to the worship of Sun God it is built in the shape of a ratha carrying the Sun God drawn by seven horses. It is an excellent example of intricate sculptural work. The chariot of the sun god with 24 wheels, each about 10 feet in diameter, with a set of spokes and elaborate carvings has seven great horses who seem to strain to pull the weight of the structure. Two stone lions guard the entrance, crushing elephants. The jagmohana is 120 feet tall and is adorned with scenes drawn from the lives of the ordinary and the royal men. There are images of Gods and Goddesses, mythical creatures, dancers and musicians, women and men socializing at many levels that are carved of soft and weathered laterite and khodalite blocks. The nata mandir in front of the jagamohana is also intricately carved. Around the base of the temple, and up the walls and roof, are carvings in the erotic style in the manner seen at Khajuraho. There are images of animals, foliage, men, warriors on horses and other interesting patterns. There are three green chlorite images of the Sun God, positioned to catch the rays of the sun at dawn, noon and sunset. These figures are carved in very high quality and resemble bronzes because of their colouring and beautiful workmanship

sections.heading: Jagannath Temple, Puri
sections.content: Puri, on the east-coast of India, in the state of Orissa is a pilgrimage center, dedicated to the Lord Jagannath. Puri has an ancient temple, enshrining the wooden image of Krishna  in the form of Jagannath along with Balabhadra (Balarama) and Subhadra, brother and sister of Krishna on both the sides. Puri is located adjacent to the sea and the vast temple complex occupies an area of over 400000 square feet, and is bounded by a 20 feet high fortified wall. This complex contains about 120 temples and shrines. The shikhara of the Jagannath temple soars to a height of 192 feet. Structurally the temple has four chambers. The outermost is the Bhogmandir, the next is the Nata-mandir, or the pillared hall for music and dance, the next is the Jagamohana - or the mandapa where devotees gather for worship and the last is the sanctum or the Deul enshrining the deities. The temple was originally built by the Kalinga ruler Anantavarman Chodaganga and later on completed by King Ananga Bhima Deva Puri is one of the four dhams or peethas of God established by Sankaracharya, the other three being Sringeri in Kanchipura, Dwarka in Gujarat, and Badrinath in the Himalayas. Shri Chaitanya, the well known bhakti saint of the fifteenth - sixteenth century popularized the worship of Jagannath. The Rath Yatra or the Chariot festival in the month June  July is a spectacular chariot festival involving the procession of three massive chariots bearing the images of Jagannath, Balarama and Subhadra through the streets of Puri . Jagannath's chariot is a 35 square feet, rising to a height of 45 feet, with 16 wheels of 7 feet diameter each. More than 4000 people drag the chariot. Thousands of devotees gather from all over the country to witness this festival. New chariots are made each year.

sections.heading: Handicrafts
sections.content: Orissa is a treasure house of opulent artistic heritage. From specimens from the temple architecture, or be it the Applique artists of Pipli or the stone carvers of Orissa. The hereditary skill of artists has handed down the ages traditional arts and crafts like weaving of Ikat, Bomkai and Sambalpuri Sari. Stone carving, applique and embroidery are equally famous, silver filigree work, palm leaf incised design, metal work, lacquered craftsmanship all have acquired a unique place worldwide.

sections.heading: Palm Leaf Painting
sections.content: disseminated. Gradually the trend to decorate the text with images began and it became an art in itself. The art form essentially consists of inscribing letters and artistic designs on palm-leaf, mostly cut into standard sizes and held together with two wooden plank covers stringed through a hole in the center. Etching is done within lines using an iron pen on leaf strips. A paste made of bean leaves, charcoal made of burnt coconut shells, seasame oil and turmeric is rubbed on the etching that highlights the figures. Colors are hardly used but if used as fillers they are in very subdued tones. Vegetable and mineral colors are used for painting. Themes are generally mythological showing figures of Gods and Goddesses complete with details of hair style and dress, animals, flowers and trees etc. Radha and Krishna, Durga, Ganesha and Saraswati are the most commonly used themes. Stories and incidents of Mahabharat, Ramayana and other epics are also etched. Scenes of nature are representated in paintings and drawings.

sections.heading: Orissa- Handicrafts- Ganjifa
sections.content: Ganjifa or the playing cards are made from circular pieces of paper on which intricate designs from the Dashavatar (the 10 Avatars of Lord Vishnu.) are hand-painted. There are ten sets of twelve cards each, housed in a colourful box. Each set is based on one of the ten incarnations of Lord Vishnu. They are painted on a canvas of three layers of gum pasted cloth and then coated with liquid chalk and polished with stone. Lacquer is applied at the back of the cards to give it stiffness. The black pigment used on the cards is obtained from soot by burning tin over a kerosene lamp. The best of ganjifa display fine lines and a pleasing delineation of features in the micro figures along with harmonised pleasing colours.

sections.heading: Applique Craft
sections.content: Pipli near Bhuvaneshwar is famous for its Applique craft. Fabrics of various colours are cut and stitched on a single colour base to form vibrant patterns. It was a craft practised for religious purposes especially for temples with embellished umbrella or fans of Lord Jagannath's as well as the auspicious temple tents. The applique work is done with great dexterity and the charming motifs include flowers, birds, animals at play and vignettes from every day life. The best of Orissa's applique work is noticeable due to the prominent usage of bold figures, flora and fauna and the use of vivid colours.

sections.heading: Orissa- Handicrafts- Silver Filigree
sections.content: Orissa is a centre of pure silver Filigree work. Pure silver ingots are put through a wire drawing machine and the hair like wires are twisted and flattened. The thin wires are pleated and flattened again to get them as thin as the original wire and then bent into various shapes to form the required shape of the designs. The space within the frame is filled with creepers, flowers, etc. The effect is incredibly delicate, almost lace like. Orissa craftsmen make beautiful silver filigree jewellery, kumkum boxes, spoons, etc.

sections.heading: Textiles
sections.content: Orissa is famous for its ikat weave or bandha which has gloriously woven and blurred, coloured motifs in silk and cotton. The intricate process involves tie and dye - knotting sections of the yarn before dipping them in colours one at a time, and finally weaving them to produce motifs in multi-hued tones. The dominant motifs in this craft include animals and birds, with the traditional designs being fish and conch shell as well as bolmala, chandankora, and sachipar. While Sambalpur is famous for its double-ikat textiles, Sonepur is known for its gold embroidered ones.

sections.heading: Orissa- Handicrafts- Patachitra
sections.content: Made on silk or on old cotton glued with paper, the Patachitra paintings are religious paintings which covers themes and events from Indian epics and Puranas. They exhibit the use of strong line and brilliant colors. Patachitras are painted in a regular series like Dashavatar of Vishnu and activities of Lord Rama and Krishna. These paintings have a basic resemblance to the old murals of Kalinga region dating back to fifth century BCE. The best Patachitra paintings are found in and around Puri, especially in the village of Raghurajpur. The artists colony, known as Chitrakar Sahi, is in the vicinity of the local temple. This art of painting on cloth can be traced back to the establishment of the shrine of Lord Jagannath at Puri in Orissa. Patachitra are made on cloth prepared with coating made from a mixture of chalk and gum. On this surface paintings are done with earth and stone colours. Apart from stories drawn from the epics popular patachitra themes are figures of Lord Jagannath, Balaram, Lord Krishna and events from His life. All this is executed in a riot of exuberant colours: dark green, lapis lazuli, parrot green, rose madder, bright oranges, yellows etc. The paintings are touched by a hint of gold and silver.

sections.heading: Orissa- Handicrafts- Stone Carving
sections.content: Soapstone and granite figures and icons are the special to Puri. Many of the figures are those of gods and goddesses, Apsaras and temple figurines. Different dance poses are beautifully executed on both granite and soapstone and brilliant craftsmenship and detailing go into the sculpting of jewellery on the figures, the fine depiction of stone trees laden with leaves, fruits, etc.

sections.heading: Woodwork
sections.content: Wood carving, a major craft of Orissa includes painted wood carvings, plain wood carvings and teak furniture. The crowning glory of artistic woodwork in Orissa is its famous sacred trio - the images of Lord Jagannath (Krishna), Balabhadra (his brother) and their sister Subhadra which are made in Puri. These figures are annually

sections.heading: Orissa- Handicrafts- Masks
sections.content: Orissa is the storehouse for brightly painted masks carved out of wood, shola pith and other indigenous materials, for use in the sahi jatra, a professional form of theatre, which takes place at the time of Ramlila, but seems to particularly highlight the death of Ravana. Some of these masks are made in papier mache. The form is taken out on a mould but the actual face, specially the expression appropriately related to each character is carefully painted in pleasing combinations of colours.

sections.heading: Orissa- Fairs & Festivals- Rathyatra
sections.content: Known as Rath yatra, this festival is celebrated in the honor of Lord Jagannath who is believed to be an incarnation of Lord Vishnu. The wooden images of Krishna, Balrama and Subhadraare taken out in procession in three chariots to their summer temple for a week. The ropes of the huge chariots are pulled by thousands of devotees. In the ancient times, devotees would occasionally throw themselves in front of the chariot of Sri Jagananath, for it was believed that to be crushed to death under its sixteen wheels was to go straight to heaven. Since Sri Jagannath is a form of Vishnu and Sri Krishna, many of the rituals observed in Puri temple are associated with events in the life of Sri Krishna. Thus this annual festival represents Sri Krishna's journey from Gokul to Mathura.

sections.heading: Odissi dance
sections.content: The Odissi dance is the classical dance of Orissa. It has a long, yet unbroken tradition that may be traced back to more than 2000 years. Dancers are found depicted in bas-reliefs in the hills of Udaygiri dating back to the first century BCE. The Natya Shastra speaks of the dance from this region and refers to it as Odra-Magadhi. Most notable people who popularised Odissi dance in the recent times are Guru Deba Prasad Das, Guru Pankaj Charan Das, Guru Raghu Dutta, and Guru Kelu Charan Mahapatra. There are a number of characteristics of the Odissi dance. The style may be seen as an accumulation of aesthetic and technical details. The Tribhangi is one of the most characteristic features of Odissi dance The concept of Tribhang divides the body into three parts, head, bust, and torso. Any posture which deals with these three elements is called tribhangi.

sections.heading: Guru Kelucharan Mohapatra dancer
sections.content: , guru and promoter of Odissi dance was born in Raghurajpur, a village near the temple town of Puri. He learnt to paint and sculpt at an early age and started playing in folk theatre groups at the age of nine. In 1994, he set up Srijan, an organisation dedicated to train students in Odissi dance. He was instrumental in projecting Odissi dance on the world stage in a big way in the early 70s and took this classical art form to a great level, His students include Sanjukta Panigrahi, Madhavi Mudgal, Protima Bedi and Sharon Lowen. Recipient of Padma Vibhushan, the second highest civilian award he died in Bhubaneshwar in April 2004. The themes of Odissi are almost exclusively religious in nature. They most commonly revolve around Krishna. The ashtapadis of Jayadevs Gita Govind are a very common theme. There are a number of musical instruments used to accompany the Odissi dance. One of the most important is the pakhawaj, also known as the madal. Other instruments which are commonly used are the bansuri (bamboo flute), the manjira (metal cymbals), the sitar and the tanpura. With numerous religions, ancient temples, local shrines, tribes and an array of sacred places, Orissa observes uncountable number of festivals and fairs round the year. Orissa has a large number of temples built in Nagara style of architecture, with distinctive features specific to this region. The three major temples Lingaraja temple at Bhubaneswar, Jagannath Temple at Puri and the Sun Temple at Konark represent the complete evolution of this style of temple architecture during the tenth century, was the peak of architectural activity. A temple in Orissa is known as a deul and it consists of a sanctorum, one or several front porches known as Jagamohana usually with pyramidal roofs, a dancing hall or the Nata Mandir and a hall of offerings called a Bhog Mandir.
